concept: Why do crowds walking in opposite directions form lanes?
title: Hallway Lanes
tagline: Two crowds, one corridor — watch order appear from chaos

science.hiddenLaw: Bidirectional pedestrian flow spontaneously self-organizes into lanes because local repulsive avoidance of oncoming individuals creates positive feedback for following same-direction predecessors, minimizing head-on collisions and maximizing throughput without central coordination.
science.plainStatement: When crowds move opposite ways, each person sidesteps oncoming people. Once a few people happen to line up behind someone going the same way, it becomes easier to follow than to keep weaving, so separate lanes emerge on their own and everyone moves faster.
misconceptions: Lanes form because they are deliberately planned, signaled, or directed by a leader — they are top-down rather than emergent from local interactions.
Lanes require a cultural rule like 'keep right' or a built-in left/right bias; without side bias lanes cannot form.
Individuals act independently so higher density always means proportionally slower flow, and lanes do not improve efficiency or reduce collisions.

sources.title: Helbing & Molnár (1995) Social force model for pedestrian dynamics. Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282
Helbing et al. (2001) Self-organizing pedestrian movement. Environment and Planning B 28, 361-383
Moussaïd et al. (2011) How simple rules determine pedestrian behavior and crowd disasters. PNAS 108, 6884-6888

story.setting: A busy transit hallway at rush hour. Dozens of commuters stream east and west through the same narrow passage.
story.mystery: Can strangers with no leader sort themselves into smooth, separate lanes?
story.goal: Adjust the crowd and watch how lanes form and flow changes.

predictions.prompt: With no leader and only local dodging, will lanes still appear?
options: Yes, lanes emerge on their own
No, need a leader to direct

predictions.prompt: If nobody prefers the right side, can lanes still form?
options: Yes, lanes form without any bias

predictions.prompt: As lanes form, what happens to head-on encounters?

transfer.setup: A fleet of warehouse robots shuttles east and west along a narrow aisle, each only programmed to veer slightly to avoid oncoming robots and stay near robots going its way.
transfer.question: What will the robots do without central control?
options: Form stable east and west lanes
Need a keep-right rule to form lanes

checks.description: With balanced counterflow and local avoidance, lane order rises from random to high, showing spontaneous segregation.
Control: Remove avoidance (avoidanceStrength=0) -> lane order stays low despite counterflow; effect disappears without cause.
Control: Remove counterflow (counterflowRatio=0) -> no lane signal; unidirectional flow does not segregate.
As lanes form, head-on collision rate trends down over time, demonstrating efficiency gain from self-organization.
Lanes still form with zero side bias, disproving that a keep-right rule is required; emergence is bias-independent.
